lines.text: If every cable on your elevator snapped at once, you'd fall about five feet.
It's Monday morning, and Gus steps into the elevator on the twentieth floor, with his neighbor.
Above them, six steel ropes hold the car, and any one of them could carry it fully packed.
The neighbor has a plan anyway. If they ever snap, just jump at the last second.
Gus does the math. A fall from the twentieth floor ends at seventy-six miles an hour. His best jump is six.
And right then, all six ropes snap.
The car drops. Gus floats. The neighbor gets ready to jump.
And one second later, the car just stops.
But wait. Nothing holds the car up. So why did it stop?
You see, a little wheel spins as fast as the car moves. Spin it too fast, and its weights fly out and trip a brake.
Ever yanked a seat belt? Pull it slowly, and it runs. Yank it, and it locks.
The brake is two steel wedges under the car. They jam against its rails, and the harder the car pulls, the harder they bite.
Luckily, they need no power, no computer, and no luck.
Unluckily, they only let go when somebody lifts the car.
So the cables snapped, and Gus fell five feet. He's fine.
He's just stuck between floors, with a neighbor who still wants to jump.
